procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Judicature at Hyderabad for the States of Telangana and Andhra Pradesh
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 17.11.2017 of the High Court of Judicature at Hyderabad in CRL P No. 10602 of 2017 granting bail to the second respondent.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: A learned single Judge of the High Court of Judicature at Hyderabad granted bail to the second respondent on 17 November 2017.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant filed a Special Leave Petition on 23 December 2017 challenging the High Court's order granting bail. The Supreme Court is hearing the appeal (Criminal Appeal No. 716 of 2018) to determine whether there are any supervening circumstances which would warrant the cancellation of the bail granted by the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in granting bail to the accused under Section 439;

facts: The complainant and the accused had an intimate relationship for nearly six months.
The complainant traveled to stay with the accused on two occasions, with the accused paying for her travel.
The complaint, alleging a false promise to marry, was filed nearly a year after the relationship ended.
The accused had previously been on anticipatory bail for eight months without any allegation of improper conduct during that period.
law: The grant of bail under Section 439 of the Criminal Procedure Code involves an exercise of judicial discretion based on the facts and circumstances of the case.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had correctly considered relevant circumstances in its decision.

Specifically, the Court noted that the delay in filing the complaint and the evidence of a prolonged intimate relationship were important factors that bore upon the defense's claim of a consensual relationship.
The Court determined that based on these circumstances, the High Court's decision to grant bail was a valid exercise of its discretion.
The Court clarified that its observations were limited to the question of bail and should not influence the trial.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's exercise of discretion in granting bail could not be faulted and, therefore, the High Court was justified in its decision.

issue.issue_text: Whether there are any supervening circumstances which would warrant the cancellation of the bail granted by the High Court.

facts: A second FIR was lodged against the accused on November 22, 2017, four days after the High Court had granted him bail.

The Court found no cogent material to indicate that the accused had been guilty of any conduct, such as misusing his liberty or violating bail conditions, that would warrant being deprived of his freedom.
law: The Court reiterated the settled legal principle that bail, once granted, should not be cancelled unless a cogent case based on a supervening event has been made out.

Supervening circumstances for cancelling bail must be of a nature that leads to the conclusion that the accused no longer deserves to be at liberty, either due to a violation of bail conditions or other conduct showing a misuse of liberty.
application: The Court explicitly considered the second FIR lodged against the accused but concluded that it was not a supervening circumstance of a nature that would warrant the cancellation of bail.
Applying the legal standard, the Court found that no case had been made out to show that the accused's conduct warranted the cancellation of his bail.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that no supervening circumstances had been made out to warrant the cancellation of the bail granted by the High Court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in granting bail to the accused under Section 439;
appellant_arguments: This is not a case involving a breach of a promise to marry.
The promise to marry was merely a complete elucidation of the facts and circumstances of the case.
respondent_arguments: The allegation that the accused had promised to marry the complainant was a matter for trial.
Whether the complainant's consent was obtained by fraud could only be established during the course of the trial.
The complainant is now trying to give up the 'promise to marry' aspect of the case, which was part of the original complaint.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there are any supervening circumstances which would warrant the cancellation of the bail granted by the High Court.
appellant_arguments: Though a charge-sheet has been filed, the investigation is still incomplete.
The accused has attempted to mislead the investigation by producing a cell phone which belonged to his daughter and not to him.
respondent_arguments: The allegation of the complainant that the accused had promised to marry her was a matter of trial and whether her consent was obtained by fraud could only be established during the course of the trial.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's order granting bail could not be faulted. Furthermore, the Court found that no supervening circumstances had been established that would justify the cancellation of the bail, as there was no credible evidence to suggest that the accused had misused his liberty or violated the conditions of his bail.
legal_tests_applied: For granting bail, courts are guided by considerations such as: the gravity of the crime, the character of the evidence, the position and status of the accused with reference to the victim and witnesses, the likelihood of the accused fleeing from justice and repeating the offence, and the possibility of his tampering with the witnesses and obstructing the course of justice.

For cancellation of bail, there must be supervening circumstances of such a nature as to lead to the conclusion that the accused does not deserve to be at liberty, either by reason of a violation of the conditions of bail or due to supervening conduct which bears upon the misuse of liberty by the accused.

Bail once granted should not be cancelled in a mechanical manner without considering whether any supervening circumstances have rendered it no longer conducive to a fair trial to allow the accused to retain his freedom by enjoying the concession of bail during the trial.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant failed to demonstrate that the High Court's order allowing the application for bail could be faulted.

The appellant failed to make out a case of supervening circumstances for the cancellation of bail, as there was no cogent material to indicate that the accused had been guilty of conduct which would warrant his being deprived of his liberty.
why_respondent_won: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's order granting bail to the accused could not be faulted.
The Court determined that no supervening circumstance had been made out to warrant the cancellation of the bail.
policy_considerations: While the liberty of the subject is an important consideration, the public interest in the proper administration of criminal justice is equally important, and the public interest of a fair trial can outweigh the personal interest of the accused if there is a possibility of the accused interdicting a fair trial.

When witnesses are not able to depose correctly in the court of law, it results in a low rate of conviction and can shake public confidence in the criminal justice delivery system, which is a larger public interest that must be given prime importance.
